blocks.raw:
<Callout>

Space planning logic is organized through functional zoning—the systematic separation of building areas into public, semi-public, private, and service zones—determined by programmatic adjacency requirements and circulation logic. Zoning creates order, minimizes circulation distance, and ensures that public spaces do not interfere with private functions or operational systems. Circulation spines and connectors organize these zones and determine how users, staff, and goods move through the building.
</Callout>

blocks.raw:
<Tip>
**Four zones mnemonic: P-S-P-S (Public, Semi-public, Private, Service)**: Public = unrestricted entry, visible, welcoming; Semi-public = authorized entry, work areas, interior; Private = restricted access, executive/clinical/administrative; Service = mechanical/loading/storage, separated from guest experience. This hierarchy organizes most buildings. Remember the logic: public at entry and perimeter (good visibility, accessibility); service independent and remote (separated from customer experience); semi-public interior (work happens away from public view); private even more restricted. This logic guides both horizontal and vertical organization.
</Tip>

blocks.raw:
<Warn>
Missing buffer zones creates operational and experience problems. When a high-end retail space has back-of-house storage visually or acoustically adjacent (hearing stockroom noise while shopping, seeing loading activity from the sleas floor), the customer perception of quality degrades. When office spaces are immediately adjacent to mechanical rooms (vibration, noise transmission), worker productivity and satisfaction decline. Buffer zones are not wasted space—they are functional necessities that enable primary zones to function effectively. Programming that omits buffer zones creates design problems that remediation cannot fully fix.
</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<Note>
Zone adjacency is not symmetric. A public zone benefits from adjacency to entry and parking. A semi-public zone benefits from proximity to public (people flow naturally from public through semi-public). A private zone benefits from isolation from public (restricted access required). A service zone must be separated from public (prevents visual/acoustic intrusion). Understanding this asymmetry prevents bad decisions like placing executive offices adjacent to public lobbies (creates surveillance, security exposure) or service areas visible from customer spaces.
</Note>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>1. **Zoning Strategy Analysis**: You are presented with a program and asked to develop a zoning strategy. "A clinic includes reception, waiting area, examination rooms, treatment room, laboratory, administrative office, and storage. Diagram the four zones and justify the positioning." Expected answer: Public zone (reception, waiting); semi-public zone (exam, treatment); private zone (administrative office); service zone (lab, storage). Justification: patients enter public area, move to semi-public for care, staff occupies private office, laboratory and storage are separate from patient areas.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>2. **Floorplan Zoning Analysis**: You are shown a floorplan and asked to identify zones and evaluate zoning logic. "This retail building has checkout at the rear, receiving dock at the front, and stock room adjacent to customer shopping area. Identify problems with this zoning." Expected answer: Customer entry should not be adjacent to loading/receiving (operational and aesthetic conflict); stock room should be semi-public or service (not customer-facing); checkout should be near exit to facilitate sleas and prevent theft.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>4. **Vertical Stacking Decision**: Multi-story projects require vertical zoning decisions. "A 60,000 SF program on an urban site suitable for 8 stories. How would you vertically stack public, semi-public, private, and service zones to optimize efficiency and user experience?" Expected strategy: Retail/lobby ground (public); office floors 2–7 (semi-public); mechanical/penthouse floor 8 (service); parking basement (service). Justification: maximizes ground-level activation, maintains office floor efficiency, hides mechanical from street view, separates parking from public entry.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <ExamTip>5. **Zone Conflict Resolution**: Scenario-based questions present conflicting requirements and ask you to resolve through zoning strategy. "An urban residential building must include ground-floor retail, residential lobbies, and mechanical systems, with limited separation distance. Design a zoning strategy that minimizes conflict between retail customers and residential tenants." Expected answer: Separate retail entry/exit from residential entry (different facades or sides of building); position residential lobby away from retail; use mechanical chases/buffer zones to reduce noise transmission between retail and lower residential floors.</ExamTip>
